title: Register a short-term rental (homestay): zoning permit or registry, business license and lodging tax
question: I want to rent out my home or a room for short stays in Charlottesville. What permit or registration do I need, and what taxes apply?
office: Neighborhood Development Services, Zoning (homestay accessory use permit); Commissioner of the Revenue (business license, lodging tax and business property)
summary: No Charlottesville short-term rental registry was found; the City regulates homestays by zoning permit. In the six residential districts that allow them, a stay under 30 days is a homestay, and the owner must live there at least 185 days a year. Get an annual NDS Zoning Accessory Use Permit in the Permit Portal: $100, due each January, valid to December 31. Limits: 6 adult guests, no sign, no meals, smoke and CO detectors and extinguishers. The Commissioner of the Revenue needs a business license ($35 or $50 below $100,000 in receipts), a yearly attestation by March 1, and a list of furnishings for business property tax. On direct bookings you collect the 9% lodging tax (filed monthly by the 20th) and 5.3% state sales tax. Platforms collect both on their bookings. If you rent more than one room, ask the local health department whether you need a state lodging permit.

steps.step: Check that your property can be a homestay
steps.who: Operator (the owner who lives in the home)
steps.how: Homestays are allowed only in the residential districts R-A, RN-A, R-B, R-C, RX-3 and RX-5. Look up your parcel's district in the City GIS Viewer. Also check that the address is inside city limits, because some Charlottesville mailing addresses are in Albemarle County, which runs its own process. You may rent the whole home, part of it, or an accessory apartment. In any other zoning district, the NDS Homestays page treats a short-term rental as a lodging facility (General Lodging in the Development Code), which has its own rules and is not covered here. Private covenants and condominium or HOA rules may also limit rentals.
steps.quote: A Homestay is a rental property that is offered for a period of less than 30 days within a residential zoning district (R-A, RN-A, R-B, R-C, RX-3, RX-5).

steps.step: Confirm you meet the owner-occupancy rule (or, as a tenant, have the owner's permission)
steps.how: The owner must use the home as a permanent residence and live there at least 185 days in each calendar year the permit covers. The Development Code is written for owners. State law (Va. Code § 15.2-983(D)) says no ordinance may refuse an operator only because the operator is a tenant or subtenant who has the owner's permission. The City says that rule applies now and that it will adjust its process. Tenants should ask NDS Zoning how to apply.
steps.deadline: At least 185 days of residence in each calendar year of the permit
steps.quote: During this period of validity, the owner of the homestay must occupy the dwelling unit as their permanent residence for a minimum of 185 days.

steps.step: Meet the homestay operating standards before you list
steps.how: Rules for every homestay: at most 6 adult overnight guests per lot per night. No exterior sign. The owner, agents and contractors may not prepare or serve food to guests. Working smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers, which guests can reach at all times. The home must meet the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code, as the City's Building Code Official decides. The Code also applies home-occupation standards 1, 2, 4 to 12, 14 and 15 to homestays (§ 3.5.2.E.2): for example, the use must stay subordinate to the residence, no more than one person besides the resident may work in it on the property at a time, there is no outside storage, and no noise, vibration or odor may reach beyond the dwelling. Those standards also limit visits by customers, clients or employees, and deliveries, to 8:00 AM to 9:00 PM; the Code does not say how that applies to overnight guests.
steps.quote: Every homestay must have working smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors, and fire extinguishers, and all equipment must be accessible to overnight guests of the homestay at all times.

steps.step: Check whether you need a Virginia Department of Health lodging permit
steps.who: Operator; the local health department (Virginia Department of Health)
steps.how: This is a state rule, separate from the City permit, and the City pages do not mention it. State law requires a hotel to be licensed under Title 35.1, and 'hotel' includes tourist homes (Va. Code §§ 35.1-1, 35.1-18). VDH's guidance says a rental might need a hotel permit if, for example, you rent more than one room for at least one night. Its permit page says residential-style rentals that meet its 'bed and breakfast facility' definition need a VDH lodging permit; that definition turns on food service, which a Charlottesville homestay may not offer. Before listing, ask your local health department whether your homestay needs a permit, especially if you rent more than one room. VDH says its human trafficking training rule for hotel employees does not apply to short-term rental properties.
steps.deadline: Before you list the rental (VDH guidance)
steps.quote: To find out if you need a permit, please contact your local health department.

steps.step: Gather proof of ownership and residence, and the responsible party's contact details
steps.who: Operator; the responsible party, if different
steps.how: You need proof that you own the property and live there permanently. The Code accepts a driver's license, voter registration card or U.S. passport, or other documents the Administrator accepts. The City's web page asks for a government-issued ID, and its May 2026 Council presentation says a voter ID is not accepted, so bring a license or passport. Give contact details for the responsible party. If that person is not the owner, they must be named and must sign the application.
steps.quote: If the owner is not the responsible party who will be responsible during the time of use as a homestay, then the responsible party must be identified and must sign the application form.

steps.step: Apply for the homestay Accessory Use Permit in the City Permit Portal and pay the fee
steps.who: Operator, through the NDS Permit Portal
steps.how: Sign in to the City Permit Portal (or create an account). Start a homestay (Accessory Use Permit) application, upload proof of residency, and pay $100 online. The City has posted a step-by-step video. By applying you agree to one inspection a year by City staff, with advance written notice. Apply before you start renting. Renewals are due every January. NDS warns that the City does not email invoices for permit or application fees unless you ask, so do not pay a fee demanded by email; pay in the Permit Portal.
steps.deadline: Homestay/Short-term Rental permits are due in January each year (renewals); new operators apply before renting
steps.quote: The application, payment ($100.00 annually) and supporting documents (proof of residency) may all be addressed in the portal.

steps.step: NDS Zoning reviews the application and decides
steps.who: Zoning Administrator (the Director of Neighborhood Development Services or a designee)
steps.how: The Administrator (the Director of NDS or a designee) decides the application under Development Code § 3.5.2.E. The Code sets no separate review procedure for Accessory Use Permits. An approved permit runs from the date of issue to December 31 of that year. If the Administrator does not act, that counts as a decision you can appeal (see escalation).
steps.deadline: Within 90 days of the request (Development Code § 5.1.6.B.1.g; Va. Code § 15.2-2286(A)(4))
steps.quote: Each Accessory Use Permit for a homestay will be valid from the date on which the permit is issued through December 31 of the calendar year in which the permit is issued.

steps.step: Apply to the Commissioner of the Revenue for a business license
steps.who: Operator; Commissioner of the Revenue, business tax office
steps.how: Fill in the Request for Business Information (Homestay) form. Its listed activity is 'Hotel Residential'. Report gross receipts as the total the guest paid, not the platform's payout, and list receipts for any rentals already made in 2023 to 2026. Send it through the Commissioner's Secure Portal (category: Business License Application) or by mail to P.O. Box 2964; the Business Tax Portal page also allows a new application in person or by email. A new license cannot be opened in the online Business Tax Portal. The office sets your classification and fee, then sends you portal credentials. In your first year the tax is based on estimated gross receipts.
steps.deadline: Applications are due within the first thirty days of establishing business (City page); state law says apply before beginning business (Va. Code § 58.1-3703.1(A)(2)(a))
steps.fee: $35.00 if gross receipts are under $50,000; $50.00 for $50,001 to $100,000; above $100,000, tax at the rate for the business classification
steps.quote: You are required to obtain a business license for each year in operation.

steps.step: File the Accommodations Provider Annual Attestation
steps.how: If every booking goes through an accommodations intermediary (Airbnb, VRBO and similar), fill in Sections 1 and 2. That exempts you from monthly lodging tax returns for the license year. If you take any bookings directly, fill in Sections 1 and 3 and file monthly returns (step s10). Submit the attestation with your business license application or renewal.
steps.deadline: This attestation is required yearly during license renewal by March 1st (the form says March 1 or the first business day in March)
steps.quote: This will exempt you from monthly reporting requirements for the given license year.

steps.step: Collect and pay the 9% lodging tax on direct bookings every month
steps.who: Operator for bookings it makes itself; the platform (accommodations intermediary) for bookings it facilitates
steps.how: For stays of under 30 consecutive days that you book yourself, charge the 9% transient occupancy tax on the total amount paid and show it separately on the bill. File and pay by the 20th of each month, in the Business Tax Portal or on the Virginia Local Transient Occupancy Tax Return with a check. Report platform-booked receipts too (no extra tax is owed on them) and attach booking documentation. If you cannot show that the platform paid the tax, you owe it yourself. File a zero return for months with no rentals. Stays of 30 days or longer are exempt. If no return arrives by the end of the month, the Commissioner sends a letter giving seven days to file before a statutory assessment. The attestation form warns that failing to collect, file and remit the tax on direct bookings would be subject to criminal penalties.
steps.deadline: Filing and payment is due on the 20th of each month (next business day if the 20th is a weekend or holiday)
steps.fee: 9% of the total amount paid; late payment: 5% penalty (minimum $2.00) and interest once 30 days past due
steps.quote: Gross receipts from direct bookings are taxed and paid.

steps.step: Account for Virginia retail sales tax on direct bookings
steps.who: Operator for direct bookings; platforms for the bookings they facilitate
steps.how: The City's lodging tax comes on top of the 5.3% Virginia Retail Sales and Use Tax. For stays you book yourself, you collect the state sales tax and pay it to the Virginia Department of Taxation. That means registering with the Department as a dealer, a state process not modeled here. Platforms collect it on the bookings they handle, but you still owe sales tax on any amount you charge the guest directly that the platform does not collect (Va. Code § 58.1-612.2(D)).
steps.fee: 5.3% (rate as stated on the City's page)
steps.quote: This is in addition to the 5.3% Virginia Retail Sales & Use Tax.

steps.step: Report the furnishings as business tangible personal property
steps.how: On the Fixed Asset Schedule, list the furniture, fixtures, computers, décor and other equipment used in the homestay, with each item's original cost and purchase date. Items you think of as personal become taxable business property once they are used in the rental. If nothing is filed, the Commissioner makes a statutory assessment. Due dates and rates are in the separate business tangible personal property return process (business_tangible_personal_property_return).
steps.deadline: On or before January 31 each year, per the Business Tax Portal page (another City page says March 15; see caveats)
steps.fee: Business tangible personal property tax, billed later by the City Treasurer (rate not modeled here)
steps.quote: Report furniture, fixtures, computers, décor, and all other equipment used in the business operation.

steps.step: Receive the business license and start hosting
steps.how: The Commissioner issues the business license once three things are done: all documents are in, NDS has approved the homestay permit, and the license payment has gone through.
steps.quote: Once all documents have been submitted, your Homestay permit approved, and your business license payment has been processed, you will be issued with a business license enabling you to conduct your homestay business.

steps.step: Stay in compliance during the year
steps.how: Allow one inspection a year after reasonable written notice. The Administrator may revoke the permit after 3 or more substantiated complaints in a calendar year, or if you fail any homestay requirement. After a revocation you cannot get a new homestay permit for the rest of that year or all of the next. A violation notice or correction order suspends any permit for the property until it is withdrawn or stayed by an appeal (Development Code § 5.4.4.B.2). A violation listed in the civil penalty schedule costs $200 for a first violation and $500 for each later one, and is in lieu of a criminal charge unless someone is injured (§ 5.4.4.D.6, E.1). Other violations can be prosecuted as a misdemeanor with a fine of up to $1,000 (§ 5.4.4.C).
steps.quote: A property owner whose Accessory Use Permit has been revoked is not eligible to receive any new Accessory Use Permits for homestays for the remaining portion of the calendar year in which the permit is revoked and for the entire succeeding calendar year.

steps.how: Reapply for the homestay permit in the Permit Portal each January, because it expires on December 31. By March 1, renew the business license in the online Business Tax Portal, which takes paperless renewals from the 2026 cycle on, and file the attestation. In 2026 the deadline was March 2 because March 1 fell on a Sunday. A license that is not renewed is statutorily assessed.
steps.deadline: Homestay permit: January; business license and attestation: by March 1 (first business day in March if March 1 is a weekend or holiday)
steps.fee: $100 permit; business license fee or tax as in step s8
steps.quote: Owners must reapply annually to maintain compliance and ensure all regulations are met.

steps.step: Close the accounts if you stop hosting
steps.how: Report the closure to the Commissioner of the Revenue on the online business change form. Otherwise the license and business property keep being assessed. Stop renewing the homestay permit.
steps.quote: Business Licenses & Business Tangible Property will be statutorily assessed each year if a filing is not received.

escalation.trigger: Notice of violation, correction order, or revocation of the homestay permit

caveats: No registry. Va. Code § 15.2-983 lets a locality create a short-term rental registry, but no Charlottesville registry was found on the City pages cited here. The City regulates homestays through the zoning Accessory Use Permit in Development Code § 3.5.2.E. The City Code itself (Municode) has not been checked, so a registry provision there cannot be ruled out.

Tenants. Development Code § 3.5.2.E covers owners who live in the home. Va. Code § 15.2-983(D) bars refusing a lessee or sublessee who has the owner's permission. The May 18, 2026 Council presentation said this was "Only required if the City amends the current ordinance", but the City's study page, updated after that meeting, says it "is applicable today" and that the City will adjust its internal process and amend the code next year. How a tenant applies, and what proof of the owner's permission the City wants, is not published.

Proof of residence. Development Code § 3.5.2.E.5.a lists a voter registration card as acceptable. The May 18, 2026 Council presentation says "A voter ID doesn't provide proof of residency", and the Homestays page asks for a government-issued ID. Use a driver's license or passport.

Permit fee. The Homestays page and the NDS Fee Schedule (row "Accessory Use Permits", $100, approved 1-Feb-24) agree on $100. The fee schedule's permit system maintenance fees sit under the Building Inspection heading as "Fee Applies to All Permits". Whether they apply to a homestay permit was not confirmed. The fee schedule's text layer scrambles its columns, so its rows were read from the PDF's table layout.

Due dates. The permit is "due in January" each year and expires December 31. No grace period was found. A new operator should apply and be approved before renting, but the pages do not say so in those words.

Permit review. The Development Code has no review procedure written for Accessory Use Permits. Permit Review (§ 5.2.10) covers tree removal, floodplain, sign and temporary use permits, and the common review procedures (§ 5.2.1) are written for applications under Articles 5 and 6. Any Administrator decision, or failure to act, can still be appealed to the Board of Zoning Appeals (§ 5.2.17.A). The Code does not say when the 30-day appeal period starts after a failure to act, so appeal promptly once the 90 days have passed.

Business license start date. The City page says applications are "due within the first thirty days of establishing business". Va. Code § 58.1-3703.1(A)(2)(a) says to apply before beginning business. Apply before the first booking to be safe.

Business license rate. Above $100,000 in gross receipts the tax is "Based on Classification". The homestay form lists the activity as "Hotel Residential". The rate for that class is not published on the pages cited here, and City Code ch. 14 (Municode) has not been checked. The fee tiers ($35 and $50) are within the $50 state cap for a locality of 25,000 or more people (Va. Code § 58.1-3703(A)). Charlottesville's population tier is not confirmed against the Weldon Cooper estimates.
Late business license penalty. State law allows up to 10 percent (Va. Code § 58.1-3703.1(A)(2)(d)). The City's actual penalty and interest for business licenses were not found on the pages read.

Lodging tax ordinance. The 9% rate comes from the City's Transient Occupancy Tax, Homestays and Business Tax Portal pages. The ordinance (City Code ch. 30, art. IX, § 30-251 et seq., cited on the attestation form) was not read. The FAQ still mentions the older 8% rate in its 2022 history. The 5% / $2.00 late penalty comes from the FAQ, not the ordinance. It is within the state cap in Va. Code § 58.1-3916.

Lodging tax forms. The Business Tax Portal page says "New businesses should complete the Transient Occupancy Tax Registration Form", and the Transient Occupancy Tax page lists that form for hotels, motels and intermediaries. The Commissioner's Homestays page lists only the business information request, the attestation and the fixed asset schedule, so the registration form is not modeled as a homestay step. The FAQ's statement that "Filing by the host IS STILL REQUIRED" dates from 2022 and predates the attestation that Va. Code § 58.1-3827(D) allows for hosts whose bookings all go through platforms.

Platforms. Under Va. Code §§ 58.1-3826(C) and (F), platforms collect the lodging tax and must report addresses and gross receipts monthly. The City's FAQ says one major platform has not provided gross receipts or addresses. It requires hosts to document platform remittances, or the host is liable. City lodging tax law reaches the county rules in Article 6 through Va. Code § 58.1-3843(C).

State sales tax. For direct bookings, hosts collect Virginia retail sales tax under Va. Code § 58.1-612.2(A), which means registering with the Virginia Department of Taxation. That state process is not covered here. The 5.3% figure is the City page's statement for Charlottesville.

Human trafficking training. The May 2026 Council presentation lists "State mandated human trafficking training" among proposed changes and says Virginia operators will have to comply with a new regulation. The indexed Va. Code § 35.1-15.1 requires training for hotel employees and excludes from "hotel" a short-term rental property as defined in § 58.1-3510.4, a definition about tangible personal property held for rental, not lodging. VDH, which enforces the rule, says in its October 29, 2024 handout: "This requirement does not apply to short term rental properties." No indexed section requiring training for short-term rental operators was found. A newer law may not be in the index, so check before relying on either.

State lodging permit. Va. Code §§ 35.1-1 and 35.1-18 require a "hotel", which includes tourist homes, to be licensed under Title 35.1. VDH's August 12, 2025 guidance says a rental "might need a hotel permit from VDH" if, among other things, more than one room is rented, and its permit page says residential-style rentals that meet the bed and breakfast facility definition (which requires food service) need a lodging permit. Whether a no-food homestay of one or more rooms needs a VDH permit was not settled, VDH's fees are not covered here, and the local health district's office was not identified. Step s4 tells the host to ask.

BZA appeal fee. The fee schedule row "BZA – Appeal/Variance" prints "$100/$250" and does not say which amount is for an appeal. No BZA appeal application form was found. The Board's page on the City boards site refuses automated readers, so it is not described here.

Violation appeal period. Development Code § 5.4.4.B.5 sets 10 days, not 30, for violations involving "Occupancy requirements in residential zones" and "Home occupation or office of resident regulations in residential zones". Homestays must follow the home-occupation standards. Whether a given homestay notice carries the 10-day period depends on the notice, so act within 10 days to be safe.

Civil penalty schedule. Development Code § 5.4.4.E.1 lists scheduled violations, including any use "not authorized either as a matter of right or by special use permit". Which item a homestay violation falls under is not stated, nor whether homestay rules are a scheduled violation at all.

Business tangible property due date. The Business Tax Portal page says January 31. The Business Personal Property Tax page has said March 15 (see business_tangible_personal_property_return). The Homestays page gives no date.

Versions. The Homestays page links the 2023 Development Code PDF (DocumentCenter/View/11104). This page cites the March 23, 2026 update (View/16092, amended February 17, 2026), linked from the Zoning page. The homestay text in § 3.5.2.E reads the same in both. Open US Law's copy marks Va. Code § 15.2-2286 as effective until January 1, 2027 and has no successor text, so re-check it after that date.

Not observed. The Permit Portal needs an account, so the application screens, document upload and payment steps were not seen. The City's step-by-step video is on YouTube and was not reviewed. Whether a building permit or certificate of occupancy is needed for a homestay was not found. The Building Code Official decides building-code compliance.

Out of scope. Short-term rentals in districts other than the six residential districts are General Lodging uses (the NDS page cites the permitted use table in Development Code § 3.2.2; the use standards are in § 3.4.4) and must meet the Building Code; they are not modeled here. Charlottesville's separate "Short Term Daily Rental Tax" is for equipment rentals (Va. Code § 58.1-3510.4 et seq.), not lodging.

Private rules. Va. Code § 15.2-983(E) keeps recorded covenants, condominium instruments and property owners' association declarations in force. They may bar or limit rentals even where the City permits them.

removed: Va. Code § 58.1-3706(A) quote "shall be imposed on any person whose gross receipts from a business, profession or occupation subject to licensure are less than: ...": verbatim, but it started after the words "no local license tax", so on its own it said the opposite of the statute. It was replaced with the sentence of § 58.1-3706(A) that lets a locality tax receipts above $100,000 or $50,000, and its role changed from exception to fee.
corrections: Quotes: all 74 draft quotes are verbatim. The 32 state-law quotes match I.text_of for the cited sections (whitespace normalised only). The 42 local quotes were found again in the official pages and PDFs, fetched read-only with the project User-Agent and at least 1.6 seconds between requests: City pages 1928, 1939, 1935, 1944, 186, 1488, 1345, 268 and 261, the FAQ (TID=76), news item 2455, DocumentCenter 16092, 9634, 14503, 14356, 217 and 10601, and the Council presentation (CivicClerk attachment 7229, read through the CivicClerk API). Four apostrophe misses in a first automated pass were an encoding artefact of the PDF text tool, not quote errors. The fee schedule's scrambled text layer was checked against rendered page images: 'Accessory Use Permits' $100 (1-Feb-24) and 'BZA – Appeal/Variance' $100/$250 are right. One quote was replaced (see removed) and 3 quotes were added and checked, for 77 quotes in the file and 78 checks in all. The 22 short quotes inside caveats were also confirmed against their sources.

Added step s4 (old steps s4 to s15 are now s5 to s16, and the two cross-references were updated): ask the local health department whether a VDH lodging permit is needed. Va. Code § 35.1-18 requires a hotel to be licensed, § 35.1-1 counts tourist homes as hotels, and VDH guidance says a rental 'might' need a hotel permit, for example when more than one room is rented. Both sections were added to legal_basis, and three VDH pages to sources. The summary now mentions it.
Summary: 'Charlottesville has no short-term rental registry' was stronger than the evidence, since the City Code was not read. It now says no registry was found.
s1: 'a mixed-use or other non-residential district' could be read to include RX-3 and RX-5, which do allow homestays. It now says any other zoning district, as the NDS page does.

s3: added the home-occupation standards that § 3.5.2.E.2 applies to homestays: no more than one person besides the resident working on the property at a time, and the 8:00 AM to 9:00 PM limit on visits and deliveries, noting that the Code does not say how it applies to guests.
s6 (the permit application): added the NDS warning that the City does not email invoices for permit fees unless asked, so fees should be paid only in the Permit Portal.

s7 (the NDS decision): 'approves it, approves it with conditions, or denies it' is not in the Code for Accessory Use Permits. The Code has no procedure for them; Permit Review (§ 5.2.10) lists other permits only. It now says the Administrator decides under § 3.5.2.E.
s8 (the business license): added the Business Tax Portal page's in-person and email options for a new application.
s10 (lodging tax): added the seven-day letter before a statutory assessment (FAQ) and the attestation form's warning of criminal penalties for not collecting, filing and remitting.
s11 (sales tax): added Va. Code § 58.1-612.2(D): the host still owes sales tax on any amount charged directly that the platform does not collect.

s14 (compliance): 'civil penalties ... or a misdemeanor charge' ignored § 5.4.4.D.6, which makes a scheduled civil penalty in lieu of criminal prosecution. Now: a scheduled violation costs $200 and then $500; other violations can be a misdemeanor with a fine of up to $1,000 (§ 5.4.4.C). Added that a violation notice suspends any permit for the property until it is withdrawn or stayed by an appeal (§ 5.4.4.B.2).

s15 (renewal): the attestation is no longer said to be filed in the Business Tax Portal, which the pages do not say. The license is renewed in the portal, and the attestation is filed, both by March 1.

Escalation: rung 5's trigger 'or does not decide within 90 days of filing' implied a court petition when the BZA misses its deadline. Va. Code § 15.2-2312 sets the 90 days, but § 15.2-2314 allows a petition only from a final decision, so that part was removed and the deadline now says the statute does not state a remedy. The petition must also be served on the BZA secretary. Rung 1's trigger now reads 'denied (or conditions imposed that you dispute)'. Rung 10 adds the fourth period in § 58.1-3984(A): one year from a final determination under § 58.1-3981.

Caveats: tenants (the May 18, 2026 presentation said the tenant rule was 'Only required if the City amends the current ordinance'; the study page, updated afterwards, says it 'is applicable today'). Trafficking training: § 35.1-15.1 excludes 'short-term rental property' as defined in § 58.1-3510.4, which defines equipment rental property, not lodging; VDH's handout says the rule does not apply to short-term rental properties. New caveats on the state lodging permit, on lodging tax forms (the Business Tax Portal page names a TOT Registration Form that the Homestays page does not list; the FAQ's 2022 'Filing by the host IS STILL REQUIRED' predates the attestation) and on permit review. The out-of-scope caveat now gives both § 3.2.2 (NDS page) and § 3.4.4 (use standards).

Confirmed unchanged: the six districts, the 185 days, the 6 adult guests, the sign, food and safety rules, the $100 permit (Homestays page and fee schedule), due in January and valid to December 31; the license fees $35 and $50; the 9% lodging tax due the 20th; the 5% / $2.00 penalty; the 5.3% sales tax; the attestation by March 1 (March 2 in 2026); business property by January 31 on the portal page; the BZA appeal in 30 days (10 days for the listed violations); the Circuit Court in 30 days; the license appeal ladder (one year, 90 days, court). The 2023 Development Code PDF (View/11104) was fetched, and its § 3.5.2.E text is the same as in the 2026 PDF. Contacts are office channels only: the City phone lines, the str@ and citycorbiz@ mailboxes, the portals and the office addresses. No staff names are recorded. The JSON is valid; step ids s1 to s16 are unique and sequential; the form ids referenced (f1 to f6) all exist.
open_issues: City Code (Municode) not read: whether it has a registry, the license tax rate above $100,000 for the Hotel Residential class, the City's late penalty and interest for business licenses, and the lodging tax ordinance text (§ 30-251 et seq.). The steps send the host to the business tax office for the rate.

VDH lodging permit: whether a no-food homestay (one room, or several) needs a VDH hotel permit is not settled. VDH says it 'might' and to ask the local health department; the fees and the local health district office were not researched. Step s4 tells the host to ask before listing.
Tenant operators: the City says the state rule applies now, but has not published how a tenant applies or what proof of the owner's permission it wants. Step s2 tells tenants to ask NDS Zoning.

Business tangible property due date: January 31 (Business Tax Portal page) against March 15 (Business Personal Property Tax page). The step advises January 31, so following it cannot make a filing late.
BZA appeal fee: the fee schedule prints $100/$250 for 'BZA – Appeal/Variance' without saying which is the appeal fee; no BZA appeal form was found.

Not observed: the Permit Portal application screens (they need an account), the City's video, the Business Tax Portal and the bizchange form beyond their instruction pages, and Virginia Tax dealer registration.

Va. Code § 15.2-2286 is indexed as effective until January 1, 2027, with no successor text; re-check the zoning administrator's 90-day rule and the violation appeal periods after that date. The human trafficking 'new regulation' named in the Council presentation was not found in the index.
